title: Errors
summary: Throwing, catching, naming and rethrowing errors, and how finally shapes the order of execution.

concepts.title: finally and the order of execution

misconceptions.description: Believes catch only receives Error objects, so a thrown string or number goes uncaught.
Believes statements after a throw in the same block still run.
Believes a throw only skips the current loop pass instead of leaving the whole try block.
Believes changes made inside try are undone when an error is thrown.
Believes a loop stops for good once a catch inside it has run.
Believes reading a property of undefined gives undefined instead of throwing.
Believes an undeclared name and a misused value throw the same error type.
Believes reading a name that was never declared gives undefined.
Believes finally does not run, or runs late, when try leaves with return, break or continue.
Reads the value from an earlier or later pass of the line being traced.
Believes finally runs only after an error, or instead of catch.
Believes an error subclass gets its class name as name, or has no name.
Believes a subclass constructor may use this before super(), or that its errors escape try.
Believes a throw inside catch is ignored, or that the outer catch gets the first value.

conceptCard.title: throw hands a value to catch
conceptCard.body: throw stops the current code at once and hands a value to the nearest catch. Put risky code in try. If nothing throws, catch is skipped. Any value can be thrown, not only error objects.

conceptCard.title: Errors have a name
conceptCard.body: Every error has a name that tells the kind of failure. TypeError means a value was used in a way its type does not allow, such as reading a property of undefined. ReferenceError means a name does not exist. RangeError means a number is out of range.

conceptCard.title: finally always runs
conceptCard.body: finally runs after try and catch, whether or not something was thrown. It also runs when try leaves early with return, break or continue. Use it for cleanup that must always happen. A return inside finally replaces any earlier result.

conceptCard.title: Your own error kinds
conceptCard.body: A class that extends Error makes errors of your own kind. Call super() before using this, then add properties. The name stays Error until you assign it. To pass on an error that catch cannot handle, throw it again.

A string can be thrown and caught like any other value. An error object is not required for catch to run.

items.prompt: What does packed hold right after line 9 runs?

options.feedback: Right. Items 3 and 2 were added before the throw. Changes made inside try stay when catch runs.
That adds the 4 as well. The throw ends the whole loop, not just one pass, so 4 is never reached.
Work done in try is not undone when an error is thrown. packed keeps the values added before the throw.

items.explanation: The loop adds 3 and 2, then meets 0 and throws. The loop ends, and catch sees packed as 5, since earlier changes stay.
hints: Follow the loop pass by pass until the throw.
A throw leaves the whole try block, loop included.

items.prompt: Fill the blanks so the program prints 4, then stopped: odd.

options.feedback: Right. throw leaves half and sends 'odd' to the nearest catch.
Right. This keyword opens the block that receives the thrown value.
return would hand 'odd' back as a normal result, and no error would reach catch.
finally cannot receive a value. It has no parameter, so this does not run as intended.
try cannot follow a closing brace here, and it cannot receive a value either.

items.explanation: half(8) returns 4. For 5, the first blank must throw so the call stops, and the second blank must be catch, which receives 'odd' in why.
hints: Line 3 should stop half. Which keyword does that with a value?
Raising a problem and receiving it use two different keywords.
The first blank leaves the function with 'odd'; the second blank opens the receiver.

items.prompt: A group of nine should end up in the catch block. Tap the line that fails to send it there, then pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. throw leaves seatsFor and the try block, so catch runs.
An error object that is only returned is just a value. Nothing is thrown, so catch is never reached.
That prints a note and the function carries on. It does not leave the try block.

items.explanation: return gives a normal result, so the caller carries on and prints seated. Only throw jumps to catch, whatever value it sends.
hints: Look at what line 3 does when the group is too big.
A returned value is a normal result. Only throw triggers catch.
Replace the line with the statement that raises the problem.

items.prompt: Write the body of safeLength(item). Return the length of item.name; if reading it throws an error, return 0 instead.
items.explanation: Reading name of an item with no name gives undefined, and reading length of undefined throws a TypeError. try and catch turn that failure into 0.
hints: What happens when item.name is missing?
Wrap the risky read in try and give catch a fallback.

cart exists, so no name is missing. The failure is a value used the wrong way, which is a different error type.

items.prompt: Which statement about this program is true?

options.text: basket is declared, so reading it gives undefined. crate was never declared, so reading it throws a ReferenceError.
options.feedback: Right. Only a name that does not exist at all causes a ReferenceError.

options.text: crate is read as undefined, like basket, so no error is thrown.
options.feedback: An undeclared name is not the same as a variable holding undefined. Reading it throws.

options.text: Both reads throw a TypeError, because neither name holds a usable value.
options.feedback: basket prints undefined without any error. And a name that does not exist has its own error type.

items.explanation: A declared variable without a value reads as undefined and does not throw. A name that was never declared throws a ReferenceError when read.

One name exists, the other does not.

items.prompt: How many names has upper counted once line 6 has run twice?

options.feedback: Right. fig and oak were converted. null threw before line 6, and the loop moved on to oak.
The loop does not stop at the error. Once catch has run, the next name is processed.
Line 6 comes after the call that throws, so it is skipped for null and the count does not reach 3.

items.explanation: null.toUpperCase() throws a TypeError before line 6 can run, and catch prints the name. The loop then goes on, so line 6 runs for oak as its second visit.
hints: Which names make line 5 throw?
A throw skips the rest of try, but the loop continues afterwards.
Line 6 runs for fig, skips null and runs again for oak.

items.prompt: Order the lines so the program prints TypeError: ready > open.
items.explanation: step is set first and extended inside try. step.size is undefined, so reading its length throws before the shut line runs, and catch prints the name and the text.

items.prompt: A volume above 10 should be reported as an out-of-range error, and catch prints its name. Tap the line that names the wrong type, then pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. RangeError is the built-in type for a number outside its allowed range.
ReferenceError is for names that do not exist. The level exists, so this still names the wrong type.
The text is only the message. The name of an Error stays Error whatever words you pass in.

items.explanation: e.name shows which constructor made the error. A value outside its allowed range should use RangeError, so the constructor itself must change.
hints: Look at which error type line 3 creates.
Each built-in type has a name that says what kind of failure it is.
The failure here is a number outside its allowed range.

options.text: finally runs on both passes. catch runs only on the pass where something was thrown.
options.feedback: Right. finally is cleanup that runs whether or not an error happened.

options.feedback: finally does not depend on an error. It runs after a normal pass as well.

options.feedback: Right. finally runs after catch decides what to return, so closed prints before the result.

With false nothing is thrown, so the result is saved, not the failure text.
A second catch cannot follow the first, and it would not run after it anyway.

items.prompt: The outer catch should report the error code, but the inner catch ends the story. Tap the line that stops the error there, then pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. Rethrowing the same object lets the outer catch read its code.
A rethrow must pass on the caught object. A bare number has no code property, so the outer line would show undefined.
return ends the function normally. The outer catch is never reached, and the caught object is only printed.

items.prompt: Write describe(n). Define Over extending Error, saving n as this.limit. In try, throw it when n > 10; catch returns 'limit ' + e.limit. Otherwise return 'ok ' + n.

Call super() before touching this.
